summary: Discusses the properties, applicability and operational considerations of Routing in Fat Trees in different network scenarios. It is a rough guide on how RIFT can simplify routing operations in Clos topologies and variations.

eli5.summary: This is a how-to-and-when-to guide for using RIFT, which is a way for data center switches to find routes.

subtitle: How to apply RIFT, a protocol designed for data center fabrics

tldr.problem: Data centers and other large networks use spine-and-leaf (Clos) topologies, but traditional routing protocols designed for irregular networks cause excessive flooding, waste forwarding table space, and require extensive manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees, defined in RFC 9692) combines link-state routing northbound with distance-vector southbound, automatically detects topology, supports zero-touch provisioning, and localizes the routing information each node needs to its own level.
tldr.outcome: RIFT simplifies operations, reduces failure impact, enables automated miscabling detection, and works in data centers, metro networks, building cabling, and other Clos variants.

facts.label: Minimum configuration
facts.value: Mark ToF nodes only; ZTP auto-discovers levels

facts.label: Failure detection
facts.value: Per-link BFD and three-way adjacency handshakes

facts.label: Routing aggregation
facts.value: Full on leaves; more-specific on failures

facts.label: Blast radius
facts.value: Limited to affected level and levels above

today: RFC 9696 is Informational and provides the current applicability guidance for RIFT deployments. It has not been obsoleted and remains the authoritative reference for using RIFT in operational networks.

sections.title: The RIFT Protocol for Clos Topologies
sections.content:
RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees, specified in RFC 9692) is a dynamic routing protocol designed specifically for Clos, Fat Tree, and other anisotropic topologies. Traditional routing protocols like OSPF and OSPFv3 were built for irregular networks and do not fit the regular, hierarchical nature of data center fabrics.

RIFT operates asymmetrically: when pointing north (toward the top), it floods link-state information like OSPF; when pointing south (toward the bottom), it operates like a distance-vector protocol, typically advertising a default route. This hybrid approach minimizes flooding, keeps forwarding tables small on leaf nodes, and provides automatic topology detection. The protocol also includes Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP) to auto-discover levels without manual configuration.
sections.eli5: RIFT is built for networks shaped like a pyramid. It talks up using detailed maps but talks down using simple directions. This saves work and memory.

sections.title: Topologies and Use Cases
sections.content:
RIFT is primarily designed for data center IP fabrics, where it significantly simplifies operations compared to extensive proprietary provisioning solutions. It is equally suited to metro networks, building cabling, internal router switching fabrics, and Cloud Central Office (CloudCO) architectures. Any network structured as a folded spine-and-leaf topology, with or without Points of Delivery (PoDs) and multi-plane variants, can use RIFT.

RIFT also generalizes to any Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with a clear sense of direction. However, DAGs require a companion protocol to establish the logical structure beforehand, whereas Clos topologies are known and fixed. For maximum benefits, RIFT works best in topologies where the majority of nodes are leaves and where most flows traverse upward through spines to a Top of Fabric (ToF) before descending.
sections.eli5: RIFT works in data centers, metro networks, office buildings, and other pyramid-shaped networks. It can even adapt to other directed graph shapes if you set up the structure first.

sections.title: RIFT Northbound and Southbound Operations
sections.content:
RIFT divides the topology into north and south halves. Northbound, each level floods full link-state topology information (North Topology Information Elements, N-TIEs) to its parents so that every node learns the complete structure of all levels below it. A spine node knows the topology of all leaves, and a ToF node knows the entire fabric.

Southbound, the protocol operates hop-by-hop like a distance-vector protocol, advertising routes southward only. Normally, each ToF node advertises a default route southward; each spine re-advertises that default route to its children. This approach keeps southbound routing simple: a leaf only needs to know its parent spine, not the entire network. South Reflection allows nodes at the same level without horizontal links to learn about each other by reflecting South TIEs northward, enabling automatic failover without east-west links.
sections.eli5: RIFT sends detailed maps going upward so the top knows everything. Going downward, it sends simple directions: head north to this spine. This keeps the leaves from being overwhelmed with information.

sections.title: Automatic Failover and Disaggregation
sections.content:
RIFT automatically detects link and node failures through its adjacency protocols. When a failure occurs, the protocol uses disaggregation to advertise more-specific routes southbound, steering traffic around the failure. Positive disaggregation explicitly advertises reachable prefixes; negative disaggregation explicitly blocks reachable prefixes to repel traffic away from them.

For example, if a link between two spine nodes fails, one spine can detect the failure through south-reflected TIEs and advertise more-specific prefixes downstream to direct traffic away from the broken path. This mechanism prevents black-holing and suboptimal routing automatically, without manual intervention. The process is recursive: if a ToF node detects multiple failures, it can disaggregate multiple prefixes to guide traffic through surviving paths.
sections.eli5: When a link breaks, RIFT notices right away and tells the switches: do not send traffic this way anymore. It adjusts the routes automatically without anyone having to fix them by hand.

sections.title: Operational Considerations and Features
sections.content:
RIFT provides Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP), where each node discovers its own level in the fabric automatically by observing its peers' advertised levels. An administrator only needs to mark ToF nodes with the TOP_OF_FABRIC flag; the rest self-organize. RIFT also detects common miscabling errors, such as when a node is connected to the wrong level, and reports them via alarms.

Other operational strengths include automatic Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) negotiation per link, allowing link-speed validation without Link Aggregation Group (LAG) hiding, valley-free routing that guarantees loop-free paths with at most one direction change, and minimal blast radius on failures where only the affected domain recalculates routes. RIFT includes a key-value store mechanism for future distributed applications, and supports in-band reachability via loopback injection and out-of-band reachability through a management network.
sections.eli5: RIFT switches configure themselves, spot when they are plugged in wrong, check links are working, avoid loops, and stay stable when something breaks nearby.

sections.title: Special Scenarios and Deployments
sections.content:
RIFT handles several special cases. South Reflection allows redundancy without requiring east-west horizontal links at every level. Multicast and Broadcast can be implemented by treating them like any other prefix and flooding them bidirectionally where needed. Dual-homing servers (where a server is connected to two leaves) are naturally supported; the server simply sends through whichever connection succeeds.

RIFT can coexist with controllers for overlay services or zero-touch provisioning of VLANs. It supports both IPv4 over IPv6 deployments and internet connectivity whether the default route originates at leaves (for internet egress) or at ToF nodes (for internet ingress). RIFT also works for IoT devices at the leaf level and incorporates automatic key management for cryptographic signing of RIFT messages to prevent spoofing and replay attacks.
sections.eli5: RIFT adapts to wireless servers that connect two ways, data center managers that want to control overlays, mixing of IPv4 and IPv6, and adds security by signing messages so bad actors cannot lie about routes.
